source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 22% of people in Austria were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
23.3% of health spending in Austria was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
1% of people in Austria reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
13% of hospital care costs in Austria were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
17% of outpatient medical care costs in Austria were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
55% of dental care costs in Austria were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
32% of pharmaceutical costs in Austria were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
Remote consultations cannot be distinguished and are included in a few countries (such as Austria from 2020, and Ireland, Japan, Latvia, the Netherlands, the Slovak Republic and Spain from 2019).
In Austria, Canada, Germany, France, Luxembourg and Switzerland, spending on general outpatient care was much lower overall, accounting for 4% or less of health spending.

This increase was particularly pronounced in Denmark, the United Kingdom, Austria and Japan, where the proportion of health spending attributed to preventive care was 7-8 percentage points above the share seen in 2013, reflecting substantial investments in public health measures related to fighting the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic.

This covers a wide range of facilities with most spending related to either medical practices including GPs and specialists (as in Austria, France and Germany) or ambulatory healthcare centres (as in Finland, Ireland and Sweden).
